properties.Location Note: Pin placed at high point of Poteau Mountain
properties.Note: "Poteau" means post or stake in French, possibly a reference to the appearance of a mountain. Early explorers and travel writers along the Arkansas, Zebulon Montgomery Pike and Thomas Nuttall, call the river, which flows through much of Arkansas until joining the Arkansas at the present site of Fort Smith, "Pottoe."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 154.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at the site of the "Petit Jean Overlook and Gravesite"
properties.Note: The legend of Petit Jean—often romanticized as the tale of a French noblewoman disguised as a cabin boy who followed her lover to the New World—is almost certainly a later embellishment. Historical evidence suggests a more grounded, though still unconfirmed, possibility: the name Petit Jean may refer to a French man killed by the Osages along with other members of his hunting party in 1732, upriver from Arkansas Post, the area where we know they were hunting (Arnold 1993, chap. 1, note 53). In the documents relating to that incident, this Petit Jean is described as a bohème, a term that in French-colonial Louisiana indicated Romani descent. Many Roma, persecuted in France, were deported to Louisiana during this period (Ostendorf 2021). Although no direct evidence ties this individual conclusively to the later place-name, the episode provides a plausible historical context for its origin.
properties.Reference: Arnold, Morris S. 1993. Colonial Arkansas, 1686–1804: A Social and Cultural History. Fayetteville: University of Arkansas Press; Ostendorf, Ann. 2021. “Louisiana Bohemians: Community, Race, and Empire.” Early American Studies 19 (4): 659–98; Marvin, Nathan E. 2025. “Looking for ‘Petit Jean’: Legacies of French-Colonial Louisiana in Arkansas.” 64 Parishes (Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities), Spring; Higgins, Donald. 2025. “Petit Jean Mountain.” Encyclopedia of Arkansas. Central Arkansas Library System. https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/petit-jean-mountain-6317/

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at heighest point in the mountain range today known as the Ozarks
properties.Note: George Featherstonhaugh, a scholar exploring the Trans-Mississippi region in 1834-1835, observed that French Canadians often abbreviated names. For instance, he noted their reference to the Arkansas Mountains as "aux Arcs," leading American travelers to adopt "Ozark" as the name for these highlands. In 1836, Senator Lewis Linn of Ste. Genevieve told the U.S. Congress that southeastern Missouri was popularly known as Ozark. Similarly, St. Louis resident Alphonso Wetmore, in his renowned 1837 Gazetteer of the State of Missouri, described the Ozark Mountains as reputable elevations. George Engelmann, a scientist and physician, traveled from St. Louis to Little Rock in 1837 and observed the Ozark forests along the Little Red River. Josiah Gregg, in his acclaimed 1844 work The Commerce of the Prairies, mentioned the craggy ridges near the Arkansas frontier, part of the Ozark Mountains. By 1853, Henry Schoolcraft's revised narratives, which detailed his expeditions into the western country, prominently featured the phrase "Ozark Mountains of Missouri and Arkansas" in the title. Walter Schroeder documents the role of French-speaking families in "opening the Ozarks," particularly along the St. Francis River Watershed. On what is today the Missouri side of the line, it was emigrants from well-established villages of the Illinois country on the west side of the river—places like New Bourbon, St. Louis, and especially Ste. Genevieve—who moved. These individuals left their overcrowded villages, where each family had to commute to their communal land in "le grand champs," to seek better opportunities. They settled in unplanned communities or on large land grants within the hilly interior to work or seek fortune, driven in part by the lead mining activities that had been a staple in the region since the mid-18th century. This mining was critical for producing lead for cannonballs, shot for hunting, and other purposes. By the time of the Louisiana Purchase, permanent settlements had flourished in the St. Francis River watershed.
properties.Reference: Morrow, Lynn. "Ozarks/Ozarks: Establishing a Regional Term." White River Valley Historical Quarterly 36, no. 2 (Fall 1996). Accessed April 1, 2024. https://thelibrary.org/lochist/periodicals/wrv/V36/N2/f96c.htm; Schroeder, Walter A. Opening the Ozarks: A Historical Geography of Missouri’s Ste. Genevieve District, 1760-1830. Columbia: University of Missouri Press, 2002.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at high point of Mazarn Mountain
properties.Note: Fred Allsopp claimed in 1937 that the place-names “Massard” and “Mazarn” (and their variant spellings) shared a common root. There is indeed a prairie near Fort Smith known as “Massard” and a mountain and stream southwest of Hot Springs more commonly referred to as “Mazarn.” Allsopp himself did not know the origin of the theory, but wrote that the name and all its variations were “supposed to be corrupted from [the French] Mont Cerne or round mountain.” This explanation has little etymological logic; moreover, no comparable geographical features appear in other Francophone regions. Perhaps a more plausible origin—consistent with many French-derived place-names in Arkansas—is a family name. One possibility is that of "T. Jean Massard, a French captain whose land grant of roughly 18,000 acres had its northern boundary along the Arkansas River in the Fort Smith area, a community identified by Nuttall during his 1819 exploration of the Arkansas River Valley." The origins of that land grant (and of its namesake) are also somewhat mysterious.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 151; Allsopp, Fred W. “Picturesque Nomenclature: An Explanation of How Some of the Peculiar Names of Arkansas Towns...Originated.” Arkansas Gazette (Little Rock), July 18, 1937; Patterson, Claude “Buddy.” “Massard Prairie.” In Encyclopedia of Arkansas. Central Arkansas Library System, 2023. https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/massard-prairie-5924/

properties.Note: Big Rock is the name of a 200-foot bluff on the Arkansas River's north bank in North Little Rock, Pulaski County. It's the river's first significant rock outcrop, 121 miles upstream from the Arkansas and Mississippi Rivers' confluence, and two miles upstream from a smaller outcrop known as Little Rock, where Arkansas' capital city developed. French explorer Jean-Baptiste Bénard de La Harpe was the first European to document the bluffs on April 9, 1722, claiming them for King Louis XIV of France. He named it “Le Rocher Français” (“French Rock”).
properties.Reference: Buck, Kate. "Big Rock." Encyclopedia of Arkansas. Central Arkansas Library System. Last modified 2024. Accessed March 29, 2024.

properties.French/Creole Root: Écores aux Pins (?) / Cabane à Joseph Bonne (?)
properties.Location Note: At present site of Joseph Bonne's cabin, corner of Barraque and Chestnut Streets in Downtown Pine Bluff
properties.Note: "French and Spanish settlers intermarried with Quapaw women and some of their descendants still live in Jefferson County. From one of these relationships came Joseph Bonne who was born in 1793 and was baptized by a visiting priest at Arkansas Post. Records dating back to 1801 show that 'fifty miles up the Arkansas River on the Bonne Reserve lived Joseph Bonne, Michael Bonne and other taxpayers named Bonne.' Joseph Bonne was interpreter for the United States government at the signing of the Quapaw Cession at St. Louis, Missouri, August 21, 1818. Due to a great flood in 1819, Bonne and his wife, Mary Imbeau, moved five miles upstream from the Bonne Reserve to the place later named Pine Bluff. This was the first bluff above the mouth of the river and was covered by towering pine trees, the eastern boundary of the coastal plain of South Arkansas. Bonne built a log cabin with a lean-to which served as his home…as well as a tavern with lodging accommodations for travelers. The settlement was officially named “The Town of Pine Bluff” by the county court on October 16, 1832." It is notable that the 1976 Jefferson County Historical Commission marker at this site describes Joseph Bonne as "one of the first white settlers"; Bonne's mother was documented to have been a Quapaw woman named Marie-Louise.
properties.Reference: City of Pine Bluff, Discover Pine Bluff, City of Pine Bluff, accessed June 15, 2025, https://www.cityofpinebluff-ar.gov/discover-pine-bluff.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed near current Peace Orchard Community Center, according to GoogleMaps (June 2025)
properties.Note: Known to early French settlers as Petit Baril—literally “Little Barrel”—this site on the Black River became later known as Peach Orchard. The name likely refers to the fruit trees planted by one of the area’s first European inhabitants, Pierre LeMieux (also known as Peter LeMew), a French settler who arrived around 1800. According to land records, LeMieux established a homestead here and planted what may have been the region’s first peach orchard, giving rise to the American name. In 1816, LeMieux deeded the property to Lewis deMun, a French émigré. LeMieux later relocated to Clover Bend.
properties.Reference: Walter E. McLeod, “Early Lawrence County History,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 3, no. 1 (1944): 37–52, https://doi.org/10.2307/40027462.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of modern-day Monroe, Louisiana
properties.Note: In 1783, Don Juan Filhiol established the first European outpost in the Ouachita River Valley, named Poste d'Ouachita. By 1785, the European population in the Ouachita District numbered only 207. Filhiol settled in Prairie des Canots (now part of Monroe), where he built Fort Miro to protect settlers from Indigenous peoples and facilitate trade. He served as commandant of Poste d'Ouachita until his retirement in 1800.
properties.Reference: Ouchley, Kelby. "Don Juan Filhiol." 64 Parishes. August 27, 2013. Accessed March 31, 2024. https://64parishes.org/entry/don-juan-filhiol.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at current site of church.
properties.Note: The oldest church (of any denomination) in Arkansas. Possibly the oldest extant building in the state and the only to survive from Arkansas Post. The Church of St. Mary’s, constructed in the 1780s, stands as a testament to that shared culture and to the lost world of Creole Arkansas–a guardian of culture amidst rapid demographic and political changes in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Despite its unassuming exterior, St. Mary’s is the oldest church building still standing–of any denomination–in the state of Arkansas. Built in 1782 amidst the War of American Independence, it was constructed of cedar atop a barge in Arkansas Post, to allow the structure to survive the many floods of the river that had washed away previous structure. It was later moved to a spot on the river near Pine Bluff and again to its current location in Plum Bayou. It was extensively renovated in the 1920s.
properties.Reference: Zakrzewski, Katie. "Mass resumes at oldest Catholic church after repairs." Arkansas Catholic, September 28, 2023. Accessed March 31, 2024. https://www.arkansas-catholic.org/news/article/7973/Mass-resumes-at-oldest-Catholic-church-after-repairs.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of cemetery
properties.Note: St. Paul’s, one of Jefferson County’s earliest Catholic churches, built about 1851 on land deeded in 1852 by Emma Kelly (Emily Callius) and still standing in 1878, served the culturally mixed Richland Township community (French, German, Spanish, Native, later Scots-Irish, English, and Italian) whose earliest burials c.1830–1840 lie in the now-unmarked 0.6-acre cemetery across today’s Highway 65—many graves lost or never marked. Among them were John Noble (b. 1798 Cumberland, Tennessee, son of Mark Noble and Catherine Elliott; d. Oct 1843 Noble Lake) and Frances Gravier (b. 1807 Arkansas Post, daughter of François A. Gravier and Suzanne Marguerite Vannoy), married 1824 at Arkansas Post, parents of at least nine children and residents about ten years in Richland Township, buried at Noble Lake—the family for whom Noble Lake and the community were named—commemorated by a 1988 Colonial Dames marker after Arkansas statehood in 1836, though many graves and stones have been lost or never marked. The first Gravier (Grabert/Greve) may have arrived in Biloxi, Miss., later moving to Arkansas Post in the mid 1700's.
properties.Reference: https://www.findagrave.com/cemetery/2342156/noble-gravier-family-cemetery; https://ancestors.familysearch.org/en/MT6C-ZGK/frances-gravier-1807-1867 (accessed Feb 17, 2026)

properties.Note: "...locally pronounced 'Barr-a-queue,' ... Antoine Barraque, a native of Gascony, France, and a veteran of the Napoleonic wars, came to Arkansas some years after the Louisiana Purchase and settled at New Gascony. He conducted the Quapaws to Red River in 1826."

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at the confluence of the Arkansas and Mississippi Rivers, at spot identified as "ghost town" of Napoleon.
properties.Note: Founded in the 1820s at the confluence of the Arkansas and Mississippi Rivers, Napoleon was envisioned as a thriving river port to rival New Orleans or St. Louis. The town owed its name to Frederick Notrebe, a prominent French-born merchant at Arkansas Post, who suggested honoring Napoleon Bonaparte. For a time, the town flourished—with a busy warehouse district, a federal marine hospital, and a post office established in 1837—but it was plagued by disease, floodwaters, and violence. During the Civil War, Union troops occupied and dismantled parts of the town; soon after, a wartime engineering shortcut—the “Napoleon Cutoff”—rerouted the Mississippi River directly into the town. By 1874, nothing remained of Napoleon but submerged ruins. Today, the town’s former site lies beneath the shifting waters of the Mississippi.
properties.Reference: Steven Teske, “Napoleon (Desha County),” Encyclopedia of Arkansas, last modified May 20, 2025, https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/napoleon-746/.

properties.Note: In the 1790s, Marie Louise, a Quapaw woman, bore two children with Michel Bonne, a trader in Arkansas who conducted business with the Quapaw. Documents identify Bonne's mother as Paduca (likely Plains Apache), suggesting she likely arrived in the region as an enslaved captive.
properties.Reference: Kathleen DuVal, “Indian Intermarriage and Métissage in Colonial Louisiana,” The William and Mary Quarterly 65, no. 2 (2008): 267–304.

properties.Note: Little Rock was sparsely populated when it became the new territorial capital, although scattered French-speaking families still lived in the area. In 1830, Father Martin of Arkansas Post conducted a census and forwarded it to his superior, Bishop Rosati of St. Louis. He estimated that there were 36 Catholics (33 "whites" and 3 "blacks") living in "Petit Rocher." The name "La Petite Roche" is a modern invention from the 1950s, and was not the term originally used by French speakers to describe the rock outcropping that gave the settlement its name.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of "Hopefield Point."
properties.Note: "Hopefield traces its origin to a Dutch immigrant named Benjamin Fooy (also spelled “Foy”), who established a Spanish encampment (Foy’s Point) in 1795, which was built to regulate river traffic and discourage American encroachment past the Mississippi River. He had been appointed by the Spanish governor of Louisiana as an agent to the local Native Americans and was also in charge of tariff collections from adjacent river traffic. Fooy and several family members had also received generous land grants from the Spanish. The settlement was renamed Campo de la Esperanza (“Camp of Hope” or “Field of Hope”) in 1797, which in turn was renamed Hopefield in 1803 after what is now Arkansas was acquired with the Louisiana Purchase."
properties.Reference: Adam Miller, “Hopefield (Crittenden County),” in Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 2023, https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/hopefield-crittenden-county-5602/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of Prairie Courthouse, DeValls Bluff
properties.Note: Named for the "Grande Prairie."  Once a vast native grassland between the White and Arkansas Rivers, the Grand Prairie was planted by the French-speaking inhabitants of the Arkansas Post in the 18th century; it was fast settled by new settlers during the U.S. period and remains a key rice-growing region despite the loss of its original prairie landscape. "Prairie" is itself a French loanword.
properties.Reference: Staff of the CALS Encyclopedia of Arkansas. "Grand Prairie." Encyclopedia of Arkansas. Central Arkansas Library System. Last modified February 6, 2025. https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/grand-prairie-5073/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at modern site "Galla Rock," according to Google Maps.
properties.Note: Galla or Galley: An old landing on the Arkansas River in Pope County. These names are believed to be corruptions of the French word galets, meaning “pebbles.” A group of Cherokee settled in the high ground upriver of Point Remove Creek and referred to their settlement as “The Galley”—perhaps itself a corruption of Galets de Rocher (pebbles of rock). Under Chief John Jolly, this became one of the more important Cherokee settlements in Arkansas. The Cherokee likely lived in close proximity to, and traded with, French-speaking traders (many of whom were of Indigenous background). A hand-drawn 1827 map of the region offers vivid evidence of these exchanges: it marks the “trading house of Alexandre, a Frenchman” on the left bank near “Indian fields,” and on the opposite bank, alongside the ferry route connecting the two sides of the military road, it identifies a prominent structure labeled “Cherokee Agency” and, next to it, a “Council Tree.”
properties.Reference: Holly Anderson, “Galley Rock (Pope County),” Encyclopedia of Arkansas, last modified November 2, 2023. https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/galley-rock-350/.; John H. Moore, Map of Dardanelle and Vicinity in 1827, Map0194, Arkansas State Archives, Little Rock, Arkansas

properties.Location Note: Pin placed along the banks of the Ouachita, in or near Frenchport, AR
properties.Note: According to local historians, Frenchport (Ouachita County) is an unincorporated community situated roughly eight miles southeast of Camden (Ouachita County). The present channel of the Ouachita River runs about two miles east of the community. Initially established near the river, the community gradually shifted westward as improved roads provided better access to Camden, with Arkansas Highway 7 now lying to the west of Frenchport. The area’s early settlers included the "Fogle," "Labeff," and "Peveto" families, who were reportedly "originally residents of France." These families journeyed to New Orleans, Louisiana, before traveling up the Mississippi, Red, Black, and Ouachita rivers; encountering a logjam on the river that halted further progress, they chose to settle in the area, and the community's name reflects the French heritage of its first settlers. Much of the surrounding land was claimed through the Federal Land Patent Office in 1860 and 1861; on September 1, 1860, John Hays acquired eighty acres, while Edward Scogin purchased 120 acres spread across three sections, with both men paying cash for their land.
properties.Reference: David Sesser, "Frenchport (Ouachita County)," Encyclopedia of Arkansas, Central Arkansas Library System, last modified October 11, 2023, accessed August 30, 2024, https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/frenchport-ouachita-county-11514/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed in the center of modern-day Pocahontas, AR
properties.Note: DeMun Township, a modern civil division in Randolph County, encompasses the area where Lewis (Louis) de Mun lived and operated mills, possibly including part of the original Davidsonville site. As Walter E. McLeod noted, “The Frenchmen, Lewis DeMunn and two or three brothers, settled on the creek which bears their name near Pocahontas, and the name Fourche de Maux (also de Thomas) is evidence of the French on that stream at an early date.”¹ While Jules de Mun (1782–1843), the French-born fur trader who married Isabella Gratiot of St. Louis, is better known, the township commemorates his brother Lewis, who came from a Saint-Domingue plantation family that fled the Haitian Revolution ca. 1799. Apprenticed to architect Benjamin Henry Latrobe, Lewis de Mun designed shallow-draft boats for Aaron Burr’s 1806 western expedition, later withdrawing to the confluence of the Spring and Black Rivers. There, by 1813, he oversaw a grist and sawmill listed as “Mun & Co.” on the 1815 Lawrence County tax rolls. In 1815, Governor William Clark appointed him to help select the county seat, leading to the establishment of Davidsonville—the first planned community in Arkansas, with courthouse, post office, and land office. De Mun eventually returned to Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, where he and his brothers became part of the region’s French Creole elite.
properties.Reference: McLeod, Walter E. “Early Lawrence County History.” Arkansas Historical Quarterly 3, no. 1 (Spring 1944): 37–52; Lawrence County Historical Society. De Mun and Company: French Connections and the Founding of Lawrence County (research presentation).
properties.Photo Credit: National Archives and Records Administration, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of "Davidsonville Historic State Park" via GoogleMaps (June 2025)
properties.Note: By the early 19th century, claims to land along the Black River were held by five French-speaking settlers—whose names are recorded as Joseph Janis, John Fayas (also known as John LaBass, Jean LeBasque, or Juan Fayas), Cola (Nicolas) LaCombe, Jerome Mattis, and Auguste Privet, when they sold their property in 1815 to Lewis DeMunn and Company. That sale cleared the way for the establishment of Davidsonville, the first county seat of Lawrence County and one of the earliest towns in what would become Arkansas. The Janis and LaBass families, among the region’s earliest settlers, were part of a larger French Creole migration from the Illinois Country and Missouri. Davidsonville was built on land sold to the government by Lewis deMun, about 8 miles south of present-day Pocahontas, at the confluence of the Black and Spring Rivers.
properties.Reference: Angela’s Attic, “Pierre Le Mieux (‘LeMew’) Family,” Angela’s Attic – RootsWeb, accessed June 14, 2025, https://sites.rootsweb.com/~angelasattic/ALL/pafg568.htm.
properties.Photo Credit: Thomas R Machnitzki (thomas@machnitzki.com), CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

properties.Note: Named for the Desruisseaux family.
properties.Reference: Morris Arnold 1986.

properties.Note: According to Thomas Nuttall (1786–1859), Derdenai was the name used by both French and American sources in the early 1800s for this rocky point along the Arkansas River in present-day Yell County. Major Stephen Long also used the forms Dardenai Eye and Dardenai, while another variation, Dardonnie, appeared in the record. One explanation links the name to the French phrase “Dors d’un œil”—translated as “sleep with one eye open”—possibly a caution to river travelers. Others suggest the name is a corruption of an Indigenous term or a variant of the surname Dardenne, as in Jean Baptiste Dardenne, a French trader who settled in what is now Franklin County. A compelling connection appears in a 1792 marriage entry in the sacramental registers of Arkansas Post, documenting Joseph Dardenne, “of legal age, resident of this parish (Arkansas Post), native of 'Up the Arkansas River,' natural son of ___ Dardenne and Louise, a Paduch Indian,” marrying Thérèse LeVasseur, “also resident of this parish, native of the Immaculate Conception of Notre Dame of Kaskaskias, Illinois, legitimate daughter of Stanislas LeVasseur and the deceased Françoise De Lacuille.” Among the witnesses was Jean Bte. Dardenne, brother of the groom. Another account credits Colonel David Brearley, an Indian agent, with renaming the area “Dardanelle” after purchasing the Point of Rocks from Joe Peran, a French hunter. Brearley was reportedly reminded of the Strait of Dardanelles in Europe and adopted the name accordingly.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 144; Vaughan, Myra, and Bishop Edward Fitzgerald. "Synopsis of Catholic Church Record of Arkansas – 1786 – 1858." In Colonial Arkansas Post Ancestry, Core Family Papers, MC 1380, box 22, file 9. University of Arkansas Libraries.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed a site marked "Clover Bend Historic District" on GoogleMaps (June 2025)
properties.Note: Pierre Le Mieux (also known as LeMew) and other French-speaking settlers first began farming along the Black River early in the nineteenth century. Le Mieux married Victoria Janis. The Janis family, originally from the Illinois Country via Quebec, had moved to the right bank of the Mississippi following British dominion over the eastern part of the former French territory of Louisiane (which included Illinois); they settled along the Black River (source). In his account of an 1824 missionary visit sent by Bishop Rosati of St. Louis, Father John Odin (future second bishop of New Orleans) and his companion, Rev. Timon (future bishop of Buffalo), both members of the Paris-based Lazarist Congregation of the Mission, which had a seminary in Missouri, recalled that 18 miles from "Davidson-ville" they stayed with "5 French families whose greatest part had never seen a priest." Clover Bend is about this distance from Davidsonville Historic State Park in Lawrence County, Arkansas.

Others say it was named after Pedro Champagnolle, a hunter/trader engaged in illegal trade with area Indians in the late 1700s. properties.Note: Locally pronounced "Barr-a-queue." Antoine Barraque, a native of Gascony, France, and a veteran of the Napoleonic Wars, arrived in Arkansas some years after the Louisiana Purchase and settled in New Gascony. He led the Quapaws to the Red River in 1826. The township that bears his name is today the site of White Bluff Power Plant nuclear facility. Antoine Barraqué signed his name with an accent. It would be pronounced Bar-a-KAY. Fred W. Allsopp adds more biographical details. According to him, Barraqué was born "on April 15, 1777, in the department of Rhin Hautes, France, near the Pyrenees mountains. At an early age he was sent to Paris to be educated in Napoleon's army, fighting in the battles of Austerlitz, Jena, Lodi and Moscow, where his only brother was killed. In 1816, he came to the United States and then to Arkansas, where he settled on the Arkansas river south of where the town of Pine Bluff is now located. He married Miss Mary T. Dardenne, the daughter of another early Arkansas family. His plantation on the Arkansas river was known as Barraque, and later formally renamed New Gascony in honor of Gascony, France. He died October 29, 1858, at the home of a son-in-law, B. F. Smith, at Pine Bluff, at 86."
properties.Reference: Fred W. Allsopp, "Picturesque Nomenclature... An Exploration of How Some of the Peculiar Names of Arkansas Towns and Counties Originated," Arkansas Gazette, July 18, 1937, https://www.geology.arkansas.gov/docs/pdf/publication/usgs_grants/written_media/miscellaneous_media/MiscMedia_PlaceNames.pdf; Community Crowdsourced Suggestion (Credit: Brandy Berendt).

properties.Location Note: Pin placed on site of Arkansas Post National Memorial
properties.Note: Arkansas Post, established in 1686 near the confluence of the Arkansas and Mississippi rivers, was the first significant European settlement in Arkansas, serving as a key trade and military post under French, Spanish, and later American control until 1821. Initially set up by Jean Couture and Jacques Cardinal under Henri de Tonti’s direction, the post facilitated trade with the Quapaw Indians but struggled due to ineffective fur trade policies. Despite early challenges, the post evolved, relocating several times for strategic and diplomatic reasons. It moved up the Arkansas River in 1749 after a Chickasaw attack, later returned closer to the Mississippi under French then Spanish rule post-Seven Years’ War, and finally shifted back to its previous location at Écores Rouges in 1779 during the Spanish period to leverage the American Revolutionary War. The post changed hands again in 1804 after the Louisiana Purchase, briefly serving as the capital of the Arkansas Territory before the capital moved to Little Rock in 1821. It gained prominence once more during the Civil War as Fort Hindman, a Confederate stronghold, until its capture and destruction by Union forces in 1863. Today, the Arkansas Post National Memorial at Écores Rouges preserves the site’s history, managed by the National Park Service with a visitor center and museum detailing its past.
properties.Reference: DuVal, Kathleen. "Arkansas Post." Encyclopedia of Arkansas. Last modified October 4, 2023. Central Arkansas Library System. Accessed March 30, 2024.

properties.Note: In 1739, Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville, erected Fort Assumption at the Wolf River as a French base of operations against the Chickasaw, then allied with the English. The fort’s name commemorated the Feast of the Assumption, the day construction began. Following a failed campaign and a negotiated peace, the French abandoned and destroyed the fort in 1740, and Bienville disbanded his Choctaw and other Native allies. Today, though the site has been overtaken by urban development, a State historical marker indicates its location. The river itself bore several names in French usage, including Rivière à Margot, Rivière de Mayot, and Rivière du Loup. One tradition, recorded in the late 17th century by the explorer Pierre-Charles Le Sueur in his Relation, recounts that Mahican guides (known as Loups, or “Wolves”), traveling with La Salle, camped here with a young girl nicknamed Margot. She is said to have fled during the night, giving rise to the name “Rivière à Margot.” Another tradition held that a Mahican guide—called “the Loup”—disappeared along the river, inspiring its alternative designation.

The French directly translated this Ogahpah name, as recorded by Father François-Xavier de Charlevoix in 1721, who wrote, "a beautiful River, which comes from the Country of the Osages, and which is called la rivière blanche." This French translation later became the English "White River."

properties.Note: In 1836, Antoine Barraqué visited Quapaw Chief Heckaton at a place referred to as Wadittesha Wattishka, or Black Clay Bayou, in January 1826. Barraqué also included the name in French as Bayou de Glaise Noire (Bayou of Black Clay). In that same year, surveyor William Pelham noted the bayou as "Bayou Wabbaseekee," describing it as "a stream with a gentle current." On an 1872 map of Jefferson County, W. H. W. Wilson spelled the bayou's name as "Water Seca." In the Quapaw language, "Wa dite" is not entirely clear, but "sha" is the suffix meaning black and  wa-tʰi-shka means creek. It is not entirely clear what French-speakers called it. Perhaps they used the French translation of the Quapaw name rendered by Barraqué.

properties.Note: Toad Suck is an unincorporated community in Perry County, Arkansas. The origin of its name is unknown and much speculation surrounds it. One possibility is that it derives from the French phrase cul-de-sac, meaning “bottom of the bag.” French speakers often used the term to describe an enclosed or dead-end inlet. When pronounced quickly, cul-de-sac can sound like “keed-suck” or “kewd-suck.” To English-speaking ears, and over time, this may have evolved into the colorful name Toad Suck. If so, the name likely referred to a narrow or enclosed section of the Arkansas River where boats could become trapped, rather than to any amphibious activity. Still, there is no substantive proof connecting “cul-de-sac” as a place-name to the area now known as Toad Suck. Alternative theories abound, such as the claim that, in steamboat days, shallow waters forced passengers to stop there for some time and a local tavern culture emerged, leading men to “suck” whiskey until they swelled up like toads.
properties.Reference: Karli New and Hayden Youngblood, “The Strange but True History of Toad Suck Daze,” Arkansas PBS, May 2, 2025, accessed June 18, 2025, https://www.myarkansaspbs.org/blog/strange-true-history-toad-suck-daze?utm_source=chatgpt.com; “Colorful Names in Arkansas History,” Arkansas.com, archived November 24, 2013, accessed June 18, 2025, https://web.archive.org/web/20131124055328/http://www.arkansas.com/things-to-do/history-heritage/colorful-names/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at approximate location of where the Sans Bois Creek meets the current banks of the Arkansas River (now flooded from a dam project).
properties.Note: "Sans Bois is a French phrase meaning "without wood." The name was given to a creek in southeastern Oklahoma with markedly little timber and later to the nearby mountains from which it flowed. It is one of the many names indicating early French exploration and influence in Oklahoma. A frontal belt of the Ouachita Mountains, the Sans Bois lie across southern Haskell and northern Latimer counties in southeastern Oklahoma. The mountains' height contrasts with contrasts the rolling hills to the south. In some areas the peaks reach more than 1,800 feet above sea level. They are composed mostly of dark shales with linear sandstone ridges that trend northeast to southwest, and the slopes are mostly covered with oak-pine-hickory forest."
properties.Reference: Brad W. Watkins, “Sans Bois Mountains,” The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, published January 15, 2010; last updated February 7, 2025; accessed June 16, 2025, https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=SA015.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at approximate location of the confluence of Sallisaw Creek and the Arkansas River
properties.Note: "The county seat of Sequoyah County [Oklahoma], Sallisaw is situated at the junction of State Highways 64 and 59 between Sallisaw Creek and Little Sallisaw Creek, at the southern edge of the Ozark Plateau twenty miles west of the Arkansas border. Interstate 40 crosses the south side of the city, which was given its name by French traders. Sallisaw derives from the French salaison, which means "salt meat" or "salt provisions." English naturalist Thomas Nuttall may have been the first to record the name "Salaiseau" in the journal of his 1819 travels in the area, then part of Arkansas. The city, elevation 531 feet, is in hilly country that reduces to sticky bottoms southward to the Arkansas River and Robert S. Kerr Lake. Nearby geographic features include Wildhorse Mountain to the south, Badger Mountain to the northwest, and Lone Pine Mountain to the northeast."
properties.Reference: Richard Mize, “Sallisaw,” The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, published January 15, 2010; last updated February 7, 2024; accessed June 16, 2025, https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=SA009.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed near the confluence of the Saline and the Glaze, near the Ouachita River
properties.Note: Antoine Barraqué, a Frenchman who settled in the region in the early 19th century and accompanied the Quapaw during their relocation to the Red River lands by the U.S. government in 1826, observed that the Quapaw referred to the Bayou de la Saline as "Wattishka Jinka," which combines the Ogahpah words for "river" and "little." As for the name "Saline," which is frequently found in South Arkansas, Dunbar and Hunter provided the best explanation in their discussion of the Saline River that flows into the Ouachita River between Ashley and Bradley counties. "It has obtained its name from the many buffalo salt licks which have been discovered in its vicinity. Although most of these licks, by digging, furnish water which holds marine salt in solution, there exists no reason for believing that many of them would produce nitre" (Quoted in Branner, 205).
properties.Reference: Antoine Barraqué to Governor George Izard. Manuscript, “Voyage of the Quapaws” [in French]. January 1, 1826. L.C. Gulley collection, MS.000064, Item 80. properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of current (2024) confluence of St. Francis and Mississippi.
properties.Note: The St. Francis River originates in Iron County, Missouri, and flows through the St. Francois Mountains before entering the Mississippi River near Helena-West Helena, Arkansas. Its course changes from a fast-flowing stream in Missouri to a slower, silt-laden one in Arkansas. Human habitation around the river dates back to around 10,000 BC. The name "St. Francis River" likely comes from Father Jacques Marquette and Louis Joliet's exploration in the 17th century, though it's unclear if it was named after St. Francis of Assisi or St. Francois Xavier.
properties.Reference: Morris, Jody. "St. Francis River." CALS Encyclopedia of Arkansas. Last updated June 30, 2023. Accessed April 1, 2024. https://www.encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/st-francis-river-2346/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at Robe Bayou inlet, east of Long Lake
properties.Note: Bayou Robe (Fr. Robe Bayou) is located east of the Cache River and west of Bayou De View, immediately west of Brinkley. Today, it is divided into Big Robe Bayou and Little Robe Bayou. In 1825, surveyors mapping the Memphis-Little Rock Road discovered the land between Bayou de View and Bayou Robe in an untouched state of nature. Its nearly isolated position had kept it unexplored, save for indigenous peoples and wildlife. Just west of the Cache, on Upper Surrounded Hill, there was once a town led by an Indian chief named Callachee along the survey route. A significant lake, formed under a bend of the Cache River, was known as "Callachee's Bay." It's uncertain whether Callachee spoke French or had a hand in naming the bayou. However, it's likely he and his community interacted with French hunters, who could have named the challenging-to-access bayou after a robe made of animal skins or a watercourse surrounded by dense thickets.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 157

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at confluence of Poteau and Arkansas rivers, in Fort Smith.
properties.Note: "Poteau" means post or stake in French, possibly a reference to the appearance of a mountain. Early explorers and travel writers along the Arkansas, Zebulon Montgomery Pike and Thomas Nuttall, call the river, which flows through much of Arkansas until joining the Arkansas at the present site of Fort Smith, "Pottoe." The Poteau River, which meets the Arkansas in Fort Smith, forms part of the current boundary between the states of Arkansas and Oklahoma.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 154.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at Google Map location of "Point Remove Park"
properties.Note: Point Remove is the name for a creek in Conway County where it joins the Arkansas River. The name comes from the French word remous, meaning “eddy” or “whirlpool.” Early American documents often refer to the site using French-inspired spellings like “Remu” or “Pointe au Remou,” suggesting a direct linguistic link to that term. Explorers and naturalists in the early 1800s—including William Lovely, Thomas Nuttall, and members of Major Long’s expedition—refer to the site as a bayou or creek associated with swirling waters. However, later writers and politicians mistakenly associated “Point Remove” with the U.S. government's Indian Removal policy. This confusion arose partly because Point Remove marked the eastern edge of Cherokee land set aside by treaty in the 1810s and '20s. But records show that the name “Point Remove” was in use well before Indian Removal was formalized as a federal policy.
properties.Reference: Larry Taylor, “Point Remove (Conway County),” Encyclopedia of Arkansas, last modified February 6, 2025, https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/point-remove-7109/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at the point marked "Point DeLuce Bayou" on GoogleMaps
properties.Note: Samuel Dorris Dickinson surmises that "Luce" or "De Luce" may refer to a French personal name. This is not a particularly common name in French. Rather, this may be a corruption of the French "Point de l'Ours," or "Bear Point." A similar corruption exists on maps of Missouri, where Loose Creek replaced "Bayou de l'Ours." If this is the case, it is noteworthy that in 1826 Antoine Barraqué refers to a stream known by the Quapaw as "Ny Wassa Jinka," which he translates as "Bayou de l'Ours." Whether that name also existed among Creoles is unclear from the manuscript, and it could not refer to the same river as that marked "DeLuce," which runs north and east of the Arkansas, as Barraqué was referring to a spot between the Ouachita and Red Rivers: "Nous sommes partis le 8 du Wachittaw et nous nous sommes rendus le même jour au Bayou que les Sauvages appellent Ny Wassa Jinka c'est-à-dire le petit Bayou de l'Ours." Literally, this would translate as ni (water) - wa-sa (black bear) - zhiⁿ-ka (little or young). Perhaps, as in many cases in Arkansas geography, the "Little Bayou of the Bear" was different from the "Bayou of the Bear."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 164; Antoine Barraqué to Governor George Izard. Manuscript, “Voyage of the Quapaws” [in French]. January 1, 1826. L.C. Gulley collection, MS.000064, Item 80. properties.Location Note: Pin placed in the middle of "Blue Mountain Lake," created by impounding the Petit Jean River (dam completed 1947)
properties.Note: The legend of Petit Jean—often romanticized as the tale of a French noblewoman disguised as a cabin boy who followed her lover to the New World—is almost certainly a later embellishment. Historical evidence suggests a more grounded, though still unconfirmed, possibility: the name Petit Jean may refer to a French man killed by the Osages along with other members of his hunting party in 1732, upriver from Arkansas Post, the area where we know they were hunting (Arnold 1993, chap. 1, note 53). In the documents relating to that incident, this Petit Jean is described as a bohème, a term that in French-colonial Louisiana indicated Romani descent. Many Roma, persecuted in France, were deported to Louisiana during this period (Ostendorf 2021). Although no direct evidence ties this individual conclusively to the later place-name, the episode provides a plausible historical context for its origin.
properties.Reference: Arnold, Morris S. 1993. Colonial Arkansas, 1686–1804: A Social and Cultural History. Fayetteville: University of Arkansas Press; Ostendorf, Ann. 2021. “Louisiana Bohemians: Community, Race, and Empire.” Early American Studies 19 (4): 659–98; Marvin, Nathan E. 2025. “Looking for ‘Petit Jean’: Legacies of French-Colonial Louisiana in Arkansas.” 64 Parishes (Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities), Spring; Higgins, Donald. 2025. “Petit Jean Mountain.” Encyclopedia of Arkansas.
