properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of Palarm Creek Park
properties.Note: Palarm Creek. Name of unknown origin. The expedition of Zebulon Pike in 1885 mentions a Baptiste Larme, a trader, and some have surmised that he is the origin of the place name. Lake Conway was created by damming Palarm Creek. Note: The stream, which empties into the Arkansas River above Little Rock, is variously rendered as 'Place des Alarmes' or 'Place des Larmes.' However, if it is truly related to a person named Larme, it would make more linguistic/phonetical sense for it to have been rendered as 'Place à Larme,' meaning roughly 'Larme's Place.' Thus, it could have been heard as 'Pa' Larme.'
properties.Reference: Staff of the CALS Encyclopedia of Arkansas. "Palarm Creek." CALS Encyclopedia of Arkansas. Last updated August 29, 2023. Accessed April 1, 2024. https://www.encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/palarm-creek-2345/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at confluence of Middle and South Forks of Ozan Creek
properties.Note: The name "Ozan" likely derives from a French term, possibly "Aux d’Han" or "Aux Anes." Similarly, the nearby prairie was known as "Prairie d’Han" or "Prairie aux Anes." In French, "Han" refers to a "caravansary" (a type of inn with a courtyard for travelers in the desert regions of Asia or North Africa), and "Anes" translates to "donkeys." "Aux" means "at" or "near." Originally, the name was applied to a stream and subsequently to a settlement along that stream.
properties.Reference: Teske, Steven. "Ozan (Hempstead County)." Butler Center for Arkansas Studies. Accessed April 1, 2024. https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/ozan-hempstead-county-7222/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at Wilbur D. Mill dam, abutting Notrebe's Bend Recreation Area, in Tichnor, Arkansas.
properties.Note: Notrebe’s Bend is named for Frederick Notrebe (c. 1780–1849), a French-born merchant, planter, and land speculator who became one of the wealthiest men in territorial Arkansas. Based at Arkansas Post, he amassed more than 5,500 acres of land across five counties and dominated the regional cotton trade through a vast network of plantations, warehouses, and enslaved laborers. A figure of Old World refinement, Notrebe entertained lavishly and was known for his commanding presence—so much so that Washington Irving is thought to have modeled the grand seigneur in his 1836 short story “The Creole Village” after him. He also played a key role in founding the town of Napoleon, at the mouth of the Arkansas River, and suggested its name in honor of Napoleon Bonaparte. Both the bend and a Confederate steamboat were later named for Notrebe.
properties.Reference: Kathleen H. Cande, “Frederick Notrebe,” Encyclopedia of Arkansas, last modified December 7, 2023, https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/frederick-notrebe-5834/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of Moro Bay State Park
properties.Note: Moro Bayou rises in northeastern Dallas County and flows south some sixty miles, forming the western boundary of Cleveland and Bradley counties, before joining Ouachita River. Moro Bay is the name of a state park at the confluence of the two streams, and one of the last of the state's free ferries crosses the Ouachita on State Highway 15. Moreau is a French surname.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 152

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at point along Menard Bayou between White and Arkansas Rivers
properties.Note: "Jean-Baptiste Ménard was a director of John Law's Arkansas colony, but he returned to New Orleans in 1722. The King's surgeon at Arkansas Post in 1768 was named Menard. J. François Menard was a prominent merchant at the Post in the late 1700s."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 163

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site where Mazarn Creek meets the Ouachita River, in present-day Lake Hamilton
properties.Note: Fred Allsopp claimed in 1937 that the place-names “Massard” and “Mazarn” (and their variant spellings) shared a common root. There is indeed a prairie near Fort Smith known as “Massard” and a mountain and stream southwest of Hot Springs more commonly referred to as “Mazarn.” Allsopp himself did not know the origin of the theory, but wrote that the name and all its variations were “supposed to be corrupted from [the French] Mont Cerne or round mountain.” This explanation has little etymological logic; moreover, no comparable geographical features appear in other Francophone regions. Perhaps a more plausible origin—consistent with many French-derived place-names in Arkansas—is a family name. One possibility is that of "T. Jean Massard, a French captain whose land grant of roughly 18,000 acres had its northern boundary along the Arkansas River in the Fort Smith area, a community identified by Nuttall during his 1819 exploration of the Arkansas River Valley." The origins of that land grant (and of its namesake) are also somewhat mysterious.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 151; Allsopp, Fred W. “Picturesque Nomenclature: An Explanation of How Some of the Peculiar Names of Arkansas Towns...Originated.” Arkansas Gazette (Little Rock), July 18, 1937; Patterson, Claude “Buddy.” “Massard Prairie.” In Encyclopedia of Arkansas. Central Arkansas Library System, 2023. https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/massard-prairie-5924/.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at point along Ouachita River marked "Marie Saline Landing"
properties.Note: In their 1804 expedition, Dunbar and Hunter mention the "marais de saline," referring to a salt marsh, near the present site of this landing in Ashley County, Arkansas.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 151

properties.Note: Little Missouri River in Pike, Clark and Nevada counties must have been named by French hunters who were reminded of the Big Missouri. But the earliest known reference to the stream in a 1778 memoir gave the Spanish version, El Pequeno Misouri. Filhiol in a 1784 report wrote Le Petit Missouri.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 162

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where Lee Creek meets the Arkansas River
properties.Note: "Lee Creek, Crawford County, earlier was called Perpillon, according to Nuttall, Papillon, according to Pike and river au Millieu, according to Wilkinson...One of the customers at the King's Warehouse in Arkansas Post in 1758 was a laborer named Jacques Papillon. Papillon might have been a nickname, for Frenchmen of the lower classes on joining the army adopted nicknames and thereafter were known by them."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 162

properties.Location Note: Pin placed along Lapile Road, in Lapile Township
properties.Note: Name of a stream and town in Union County, Arkansas. Dr. Hunter called it "Bayu de la pelle," suggesting an origin in the French term for shovel.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 150

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at current site of "Saracen Landing"
properties.Note: Saracen, also known as Sarazin, Sarasen, and Sarasin, was born around 1763 at Arkansas Post. His father, François Sarassin, served as a Quapaw interpreter for the French, while his mother, whose name is not recorded, was a Quapaw woman. Raised within the Quapaw community, Saracen experienced firsthand the displacement of his people from traditional lands to Indian Territory. He was honored as an honorary "chief" by some European Americans in the 1800s. Saracen moved back to Pine Bluff before his death and is buried there. Saracen's legacy is commemorated by the renaming of Lake Pine Bluff to Lake Saracen in 2007.
properties.Reference: "Lake Pine Bluff Renamed After American Indian Chief." Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, Associated Press, March 23, 2007; Arnold, Morris S. The Rumble of a Distant Drum: the Quapaws and the Old World Newcomers, 1673-1804, University of Arkansas Press, 2007.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed in middle of "Lake Dumond"
properties.Note: May refer to a French-Canadian migrant to the region, Louis Bernard Dumont (1777-ca. 1834). Louis Bernard Dumont was born on October 15, 1777, in Grondines, Québec, New France. He married Félicité Caillot in 1810 in Arkansas Post, Louisiana Territory. They had several children in Arkansas Territory. Louis passed away between 1833 and 1834 in Arkansas Post. Félicité, who was from Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, managed the household after Louis' death. Their children included Félicité, Louis, Pierre, Caliste, Mannet, Virginia, Reges, and Israel. Their descendants continued to live in Arkansas.
properties.Reference: Orville Boyd Jenkins, "OBJ Genealogy," accessed March 31, 2024, http://objgenealogy.com/indiI4627.html.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of "La Grue Lake"
properties.Note: The name "La Grue," meaning crane (a bird), is derived from French.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where Bayou La Grue meets the White River
properties.Note: Name of streams in Arkansas county, derived from the French word "grue," meaning crane.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 150

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where LaBaum Creek meets Moro Creek
properties.Note: "La Bum Creek, which flows into Moro Bay, Bradley County, probably got its name either from Le Bum, a Choctaw chief of a band living in the present Ouachita County in the early 1800s or else from the French family La Baume whose name in corrupted form was that of the Indian leader. Josef de la Baume, a subaltern, accompanied Don Juan Filhiol to Écore à Fabri to found the Post of Ouachita, and when the post was relocated at the site of Monroe, Louisiana, he went there and settled."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 162

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where the Boeuf River meets the Lafourche River
properties.Note: According to Encyclopedia Britannica, the "Boeuf River," also spelled "Boeuff," rises in southeastern Arkansas and flows into Louisiana, entering the Ouachita River in Catahoula Parish. Part of the river’s 230-mile course is navigable. From the French for "river of cattle." Not cows, but buffalo.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 142

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site where L'Eau Frais Creek enters the Ouachita River
properties.Note: Name of a stream in Clark County, Arkansas. Referred to by Dunbar and Hunter as "Bayau de l'eau Froide." The contemporary pronunciation among locals as "Low Freight" makes sense given that the Canadian pronunciation of the French term "froide" is "frette." Many of the hunters who settled this area came from the former territories of New France (the St. Lawrence Valley).
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 150

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at confluence of L'Anguille and St. Francis rivers
properties.Note: Name of a stream and township in St. Francis County, Arkansas, deriving from the French word "l'anguille." meaning eel.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 150

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site where Brushy L'Aigle and L'Aigle creeks meet
properties.Note: Name of streams in Bradlee County, Arkansas. Most likely named for the D'Aigle family of Arkansas Post. The 1796 census of the Post included Francisco (François) and Marie (Marie) D'Aigle and son Francisco (François)
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 150

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site where I-530 crosses over Imbeau Bayou
properties.Note: Named for the Imbeau family of the Pine Bluff and Little Rock regions.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of contemporary confluence of Illinois Bayou and Arkansas River
Pin placed at site where Gulpha Creek meets the Ouachita River
properties.Note: Creek near Hot Springs, most likely named for a person with the name Calfat (which makes the most sense given that Dunbar and Hunter identified it as "Fourche of Calfat" in their report (1805). "Calfat," in French, means caulker (a person who seals boats using pitch).
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 149

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at center of Marion, Arkansas
properties.Note: "Grandee, a lake beside which Marion was built in Crittenden County, bears the name of Augustine Grandee or Augustin Grande who settled there about 1801. Although he was only a sergeant, he was in command of Spain's Campo de Esperanza, and he delivered it to France's agent after Spain returned Louisiana to her" (Dickinson, 160). Grandee was known by multiple names, including Marion Lake. "In 1918, the lake was drained, creating between 600 and 800 new acres of farmland. All that remains of the lake is a drainage ditch" (Ralph Hardin, "Marion," Arkansas Encyclopedia, accessed 3 March 2024).
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 160

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of "Grand Marais Recreation Park"
properties.Note: Name of swamp in Union County, Arkansas, whose name derives from the French for "Great Marsh"

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at confluence of Glaze Creek and Ouachita River
properties.Note: A creek in Bradlee county that most likely derives its name from "Glaise" (salt lick)

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at the confluence of French Creek and Ouachita River.
Pin placed at site where François Creek meets the Saline River
properties.Note: "François" (pronounced in early French dialects, including in modern-day Canadian dialects as "France-way") could refer to a person or, generically, to French people.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 148

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site where Fourche La Fave meets the Arkansas River
properties.Note: Name of a river in Perry and Yell counties, Arkansas. The name appears in Stephen Long's report from his 1820 expedition to the Rocky Mountains. It is named for a prominent family of Arkansas Post, whose name (sometimes spelled "La Feve") was LeFevre. The 1791 census of the Post includes Pierre LeFevre, his wife Marie, an unnamed son, and an unnamed daughter, as well as, separately, a household belonging to Louis LeFevre. It is noteworthy that, in Canadian pronunciation, LeFevre is often pronounced with the final syllable sounding like a long “a” (as in day) or somewhere between a long “i” (as in ride) and a long “a,” while the final “-re” is not pronounced or is barely audible—approximating an English phonetic spelling such as Leuh-Five or Leuh-Fave.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 150

properties.Note: "Fourche," meaning "fork," was used throughout Louisiane to describe a small river or tributary
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 159

properties.Location Note: Pin Placed where Fourche River meets Black River, Randolph County
properties.Note: Tributary of Black River in Randolph County was "corrupted to [from] Fourche Dumas." Who Thomas (or Dumas) was is unknown.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 159

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site where Fourche à Loup creek meets modern-day Lake Hamilton
properties.Note: Meaning "Wolf Fork" (or River), a place in Garland County, Arkansas. Fourche a Loupe Creek empties into what is today Lake Hamilton, created from impounding the Ouachita River, in Hot Springs, Arkansas.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 148
properties.Photo Credit: Samuel Grant, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

properties.Location Note: The approximate latitude and longitude of the confluence where the Eleven Point River meets the Spring River.
properties.Note: Some theories suggest that the name Eleven Point River comes from early French explorers who counted eleven "pointes"—eleven distinct wooded points or bends in the river, which flows from the Missouri Ozarks into northeast Arkansas. "Pointes" was a term they used as navigational markers. A more dubious claim attributes the name to phrases like pont levé (“raised bridge”) or levé pont, but these have little linguistic or historical support.
properties.Reference: Mike Bezemek, “Mysteries of the Eleven Point River,” Terrain Magazine, August 4, 2024. https://terrain-mag.com/mysteries-of-the-eleven-point-river.
properties.Photo Credit: Charlie Llewellin, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where the Ecore Fabri Bayou meets the Ouachita River
properties.Note: Named for André Fabri de la Bruyère, notary from France, who explored this area from New Orleans. Don Juan Filhiol first placed the site of the Poste des Ouachitas here before it was moved to modern-day Monroe, Louisiana.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 148

properties.Location Note: Pin placed near the waterfront in the town of Camden, Arkansas
properties.Note: "Écore" refers to a bluff. This is the site where French explorer Fabri de la Bruyère crossed the Ouachita. The town of Camden, Arkansas is built on the bluff.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 148

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at confluence of Des Arc Bayou and White River, near site of town of Des Arc
properties.Note: Refers to the abbreviated form of the "Poste des Arkansas" (Arkansas Post). A creek of this name appears on the Zebulon Pike map of Lousiana, published in Philadelphia in 1810.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 147

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at point where Derrieusseaux Creek joins Grisly Creek
properties.Note: "The French family, whose name is spelled Der(r)ruisseaux, Deruisau and Desruisseaux first settled at Arkansas Post. Jean Baptiste DesRuisseaux signed the 1789 petition of settlers and hunters at the post, asking Commandant Josef Vallière to declare war on the Osages."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 146

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where Departee Creek meets White River
properties.Note: "Departi" means separated. Possible name for the creek.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 159

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where De Gray Creek runs into Caddo River at DeGray Regulating Lake near Caddo Valley
properties.Note: Meaning "Sandstone." The stream of this name was noted for its soft, easily cut stone. Although the name may refer to a person, perhaps not of French origin.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 146

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at point where Deceiper Creek meets the Ouachita River
properties.Note: "...from Bayu du Cypre, properly Bayou du Cyprès (Cypress Bayou). Dr. George Hunter, in his account of exploration of the Ouachita River, remarked that the cypress growing around the mouth of the bayou were noteworthy because the species seldom was seen farther north." Jeff Jeffers notes that locals pronounce the place "dee-seeper."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 146 and Joe Jeffers, “French Place Names in Clark County, Arkansas,” Articles (January 1, 2019), https://scholarlycommons.obu.edu/articles/254, 6

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site along the Miss. roughly 122 miles below confluence of Mississippi and Arkansas (per René Paul's 1818 map). Not clear that island still exists.
properties.Note: River navigation landmark. Appears on René Paul's 1818 "Map of the territorial limits of the Quapaw cession."
properties.Reference: Rene Paul, Map of the Territorial Limits of the Quapaw Cession, August 1818, UA Little Rock Center for Arkansas History and Culture Maps Records, 1712–1991 (UALR.MS.0314), University of Arkansas at Little Rock Center for Arkansas History and Culture, identifier ualr-ms-0314_03_na_na_20_map0004, https://cdm15728.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p15728coll3/id/1539.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where De Roches Creek meets Ouachita River
properties.Note: Creek in Hot Spring County, near an "island" on the Ouachita (sometimes called "Rocky Island"). Fred W. Allsopp writes that this creek "may be named for the de Roche family, early settlers in the state."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 159;  Fred W. Allsopp, "Picturesque Nomenclature... An Exploration of How Some of the Peculiar Names of Arkansas Towns and Counties Originated," Arkansas Gazette, July 18, 1937, https://www.geology.arkansas.gov/docs/pdf/publication/usgs_grants/written_media/miscellaneous_media/MiscMedia_PlaceNames.pdf

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at approximate location of current Curia Creek and Black River
properties.Note: Possibly a reference to the word for priest in French or Spanish
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 159 & Encyclopedia of Arkansas (Curia)

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at confluence of Deep Bayou and Coussart Bayou
properties.Note: "Cusotte Bayou in Jefferson and Lincoln counties has the name of a French family at Arkansas Post. Their name also is spelled Cou(s)ot. Francisco Cousot was a member of the militia at Arkansas Post in 1780. In 1816 the U.S. government rejected the claim of Francis Coussot to 760 arpents of land on the Arkansas River."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 159

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of Cossatot River South Trailhead, Cossatot River State Park
properties.Note: Casse-tête means "tomahawk" in French. Name of a stream in Sevier county.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 145

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where the Corney Bayou crosses the Arkansas/Louisiana border
properties.Note: "Cornie or Corny" Stream in Union County." Corney Bayou rises in Columbia County and flows into Bayou d'Arbonne in Union Parish, LA. Dickinson claims it derives from the French corne for horn.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 145

properties.Note: The name Shinall Mountain—a hill in West Little Rock—is a corruption of Chenault, the surname of a mid-19th-century settler family of Huguenot descent from Alabama. When Deltic Timber Corporation developed the Chenal Valley real estate project, they adopted the French-style spelling Chenal to mimic French pronunciation as part of a foreign branding strategy. The development takes its name from Shinall Mountain. In 1937, Fred W. Allsopp incorrectly attributed the name's origin to "French settlers" (Arkansas Gazette, July 18, 1937). It is possible that Chenault Island shares the same origin. While chenault resembles a French word for “oak grove,” the name more likely reflects the Chenault family, not a botanical feature.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at point where West Creek meets Chemin-A-Haut Creek
properties.Note: For centuries, First Nations people used this elevated ridge along the bayou as a pathway for hunting and trading between what is now Arkansas and Louisiana. The French adopted the route, naming it chemin-à-haut, meaning "high road." This path became the route between the Post of Ouachita and Arkansas Post, following the high ground from the Ouachita lowland.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 155.

properties.Note: "Charivari Creek and Chiver Creek are tributaries of Eagle Creek in Bradley County. The charivari (Fr. for hubbub, uproar, mock serenade) was an old wedding custom in France before the discovery of America. It was introduced into Louisiana at the beginning of the colony. Friends of a newly married couple gave them a mock serenade, often around ten o'clock at night. Pans were beaten, horns blown, and bells were rung until the husband and wife got out of bed and invited visitors to come in for refreshments. The custom was practiced in rural Arkansas until about WWII."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 158-159

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where Castor Bayou empties into Swan Lake (oxbow lake)
properties.Note: Likely derives from French word for beaver.
properties.Reference: [None]

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site where Cassa Massa Creek enters the Ouachita River
properties.Note: "Maçon's hiding place." A bayou that empties into the Ouachita River in Clark County. The name derives from the Maçon family of Oachita Post (today Monroe, Louisiana), who arrived in the area in the late eighteenth century. Some of the Maçons were hunters and traders.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 158

properties.Location Note: Terre Rouge Creek Near Prescott, Ark.
properties.Note: "Terre Rouge Creek, 'Red Earth,' draining eastern Hempstead and Nevada counties, locally is called 'Carooze'"
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 156

properties.Location Note: Near confluence with the Arkansas River, Haskell County, Oklahoma.
properties.Note: The Canadian River is the longest tributary of the Arkansas River, measuring approximately 1,216 kilometers (755 miles). It originates in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains in southern Colorado (Las Animas County) and flows east-southeast through northeastern New Mexico, the Texas Panhandle, and central to eastern Oklahoma, where it eventually joins the Arkansas River near Haskell County. The river passes through varying landscapes, including the Kiowa National Grassland in New Mexico and the Red Bed Plains of Oklahoma. It forms Lake Eufaula, one of Oklahoma’s largest reservoirs, before its confluence with the Arkansas. Historically, the Canadian River served as a key transport and trade corridor, first for Indigenous peoples (notably the Comanche, Kiowa, and Caddo), then for French explorers (such as the Mallet brothers in 1739), and later for American expeditions (like those of Zebulon Pike and John C. Frémont). It was part of overland travel routes between French Louisiana and Spanish New Mexico in the 18th century. In 1929, historian Muriel H. Wright wrote that the river may have been named around 1820 by or in reference to Canadian French fur traders camped near its confluence with the Arkansas River. However, this may reflect a local naming tradition rather than the original naming event. Sometimes called “South Canadian River” to distinguish it from the North Canadian River.
properties.Reference: “Canadian (rivière),” Wikipédia, last modified June 19, 2025, https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_(rivière).
properties.Origin Note: French-Canadian trappers, perhaps as late as the early 19th century

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where the South Caddo River meets the Caddo River
properties.Note: In the early 1800s, the Caddo River was known as "La Fourche des Cadaux" in Montgomery and Clark counties. Originating in the Ouachita Mountains, it flows through Montgomery, Pike, and Clark counties in Arkansas. The river eventually feeds into DeGray Lake, formed by the construction of DeGray Dam. The dam created a lake covering 13,400 acres with a 207-mile shoreline. Construction of DeGray Dam began late in 1962, with initial work including the construction of an access road and a concrete bridge over the Caddo River.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 143

properties.Location Note: Pin placed where the White River meets the Cache River
properties.Note: The Cache River, a 213-mile-long tributary of the White River in northeastern Arkansas, also drains a small portion of southeastern Missouri. In H.M. Brackenridge's "Views of Louisiana...Journal of a Voyage up the Missouri River in 1811," the river is referred to as "Eaux caché," meaning "Hidden Waters."
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 145; Fred W. Allsopp, "Picturesque Nomenclature... An Exploration of How Some of the Peculiar Names of Arkansas Towns and Counties Originated," Arkansas Gazette, July 18, 1937, https://www.geology.arkansas.gov/docs/pdf/publication/usgs_grants/written_media/miscellaneous_media/MiscMedia_PlaceNames.pdf.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at confluence of Bois D'Arc Bayou and Finn Bayou
properties.Note: One or more rivers in Arkansas are sometimes referred to as "Bodock," deriving from the French "bow wood" (bois d'arc), which refers to the Osage orange tree. In Arkansas, the Osage orange tree is sometimes called the "Bodark Tree." The Caddos crafted bows from this wood and traded them extensively. As a result, several streams in Arkansas were given this name.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 142

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at confluence of "Bayou Boggy" and "Bayou Macon"
properties.Note: The name of "Boggy Bayou," originates from the prominent Bogy family of Arkansas Creoles. This family, whose name was also spelled "Bougie" or "Boujee," was listed in the 1791 census of Arkansas Post. Members of the household included Joseph Bougy, his wife Marie, and their children Joseph, Charles, Louis, Catherine, and Marie.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 158

properties.Location Note: Pin placed on Little Bodcau Creek
properties.Note: In 1779, Louisiana Governor-General Esteban Miro referred to the community near Little Bodcaw as Batea. The name Bodcaw likely originated from Choctaw bokko, meaning 'mound,' giving rise to the name of the Nevada County community.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 142

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at site of Belle Isle park (Fort Smith, AR)
properties.Note: Tradition states that this promontory, named Belle Point ('Belle Pointe' in French, meaning 'Beautiful Point'), was where coureurs de bois met annually. It was selected by Major Long in fall 1817 as the site of Fort Smith. This is the name traveller Thomas Nuttall (1786–1859) uses (Belle Pointe) in the journals of his travels in 1819.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 141

properties.Location Note: Pin placed at the center of the hamlet that bears this name.
properties.Note: Bayou Meto, a stream that begins in the hills of northeast Pulaski County and southeast Faulkner County, is rich in mineral deposits, which may explain its name. One possible origin is the French word "métaux" (meaning metals), suggesting a connection to these deposits. Given the current pronunciation, "MEE-tuh," another explanation also seems plausible--that the name could derive from the phrase "mi-terre, mi-eau" (half-land, half-water), used to describe a wetland. Additionally, "mi-terre" could refer to the bayou's location between and parallel to two major thoroughfares, the Arkansas and White rivers. According to an entry in the Arkansas Encyclopedia, until the early twentieth century, “Bayou Metoe” was used with some frequency. An 1819 US Survey of a "Spanish Land Grant" accorded to Pedro (Pierre) Pertuis uses the spelling "Bayou Meteau." (Source:  Arkansas Commissioner of State Lands). These last two suggest that the "métaux" origin is the correct one.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 152; Fred W. Allsopp, “Picturesque Nomenclature: An Explanation of How Some of the Peculiar Names of Arkansas Towns...Originated,” Arkansas Gazette, July 18, 1937.

properties.Location Note: Pin placed along the Bayou Macon where it passes Eudora, Arkansas
properties.Note: A stream that originates in Desha County, Arkansas, named after the Maçon family from the area around the Ouachita Post (historically near what is today Camden, Arkansas), who settled in the late eighteenth century. Some members of the Maçon family were known as hunters and traders.
properties.Reference: Samuel Dorris Samuel Dorris Dickinson, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, “Colonial Arkansas Place Names,” The Arkansas Historical Quarterly 48, no. 2 (1989): 137–168, 151

properties.Location Note: Pin placed close to the source of Dorcheat Bayou, in Nevada County, Arkansas, around the confluence of Mill and Bushy Creeks
properties.Note: One theory was that this was possibly a corruption of the Caddo word for "people." Fred W. Allsopp makes the link with another Arkansas placename, recorded as early as the beginning of the nineteenth century: this stream, corrupted into Bayou Dache, had derived from the earlier Bayou de Hachis. The Hachis were a tribe in southern Arkansas and northern Louisiana. Bayou de Hache or Bayou de Hachis and Côte de Hachis were reported by the Dunbar and Hunter expedition as being on the west side of the Ouachita between Moro Bay and Smackover Creek.

properties.Note: Bayou Bartholomew, the longest bayou in the world, extends over 364 miles (586 km) across Arkansas and Louisiana. Historian Rebecca DeArmond-Huskey points to the earliest documented mention of the bayou, named Barthélemy since at least 1781, highlighting its significance to fugitive slaves and free people of color. In January of that year, the Arkansas Post commandant wrote to his superiors in New Orleans that a Quapaw hunter named Chalmet had recently discovered a fugitive slave, with a gun, by a fire pit on the bayou Barthélemy near the Ouachita River. During the era of Spanish colonial rule, the Quapaw were frequently paid by the regime for their role in capturing and delivering fugitive slaves, many of whom, like the man discovered in 1781, had actually run away from the lower Mississippi Valley. The bayou's name likely derives from a man named Barthélemy (not an individual from the 17th-century La Salle expedition, as indicated on the official state marker) who lived in the late 18th and early 19th centuries in the lower Arkansas River valley and who married a woman (probably enslaved) who was Plains Apache; their son appears in the documentary record, as highlighted in an article by Morris Arnold, as Charlot, a voyageur, making a trading voyage between Arkansas Post and St. Louis. The Bayou was important as an alternative route to Lower Louisiana when the Mississippi was unnavigable.

properties.Note: Antoine is situated along the Southwest Trail, leading into Texas. Local lore holds that it was named after a Frenchman whose body was discovered by a local river, as mentioned in a 1951 interview with resident Olen Hendrix. However, there's no documentary evidence to support this story. The name is more likely derived from the nearby river, named by French hunters in the late 18th century who also named the Little Missouri River. In the early 1800s, there was a French settlement in the area now known as the East Place on the Antoine. The settlers attended the Church of St. Francis Xavier, located where the First Baptist Church of Antoine stands today.
